Self-esteem and identity

Why do I compare myself with others so much?

Comparing ourselves is almost unavoidable: it is one of the ways we gauge how we are doing. The problem is with whom and with what.

You see that a friend has been promoted, an acquaintance runs marathons or someone your age has a beautiful home, and something stirs inside you. Comparing ourselves with others is one of the most human things there is.

Social comparison theory

In 1954, the psychologist Leon Festinger proposed that when we have no objective measure of our abilities or opinions, we evaluate ourselves by comparing with other people, especially those similar to us. Comparison can help us learn and get motivated, but it can also drag us down.

Research distinguishes upward comparison, with people doing better, which can inspire or discourage, and downward comparison, with people doing worse, which can console or make us feel superior. On social media, upward comparison is constant, because we see the best of other people's lives, selected and polished. A 2014 study found that heavier Facebook users made more upward comparisons and had lower self-esteem.

Upwards and downwards

Not all comparisons are the same. Comparing yourself with someone better off, an upward comparison, can inspire if the goal seems reachable, or discourage if it seems impossible. Comparing yourself with someone worse off, a downward comparison, can comfort in hard times; Shelley Taylor's studies of women with breast cancer showed that many compared themselves with patients in a worse situation to feel stronger. What hurts most is comparing yourself only upwards, with unrealistic models.

Other people's edited lives

On social media we tend to compare our everyday lives, with their dull and bad moments, with other people's best moments, chosen and polished. Several studies find that passive use, scrolling through posts without interacting, is associated with more envy and worse mood than active use to communicate with people close to us.

What usually helps

  • Remember you are comparing your whole life with a shop window. Others have doubts and problems they do not post.
  • Compare yourself with yourself: what have you learned or improved compared with a year ago?
  • Use comparison as information: if someone has something you want, ask what steps you could take, instead of getting stuck in envy.
  • Cut down exposure to accounts that make you feel worse.

References

  1. Festinger, L. (1954). A theory of social comparison processes. Human Relations, 7(2), 117–140.
  2. Vogel, E. A. et al. (2014). Social comparison, social media, and self-esteem. Psychology of Popular Media Culture, 3(4), 206–222.
  3. Taylor, S. E. y Lobel, M. (1989). Social comparison activity under threat: downward evaluation and upward contacts. Psychological Review, 96(4), 569–575.
  4. Verduyn, P. et al. (2017). Do social network sites enhance or undermine subjective well-being? A critical review. Social Issues and Policy Review, 11(1), 274–302.
